newsitem.title: USA: House votes to end federal arts funding.
newsitem.headline: House votes to end federal arts funding.

text.p: The House Friday rejected a plan to continue federal funding for the arts through grants to states and school districts, one day after it moved to abolish the National Endowment for the Arts.
The House voted 271-155 against a compromise offered by House Republicans that would have replaced the NEA with a system of block grants administered mostly by the Education Department.

The deal was foiled by Democrats and a number of moderate Republicans who refused to vote for a scheme to shut down the NEA, and by many conservative Republicans who balked at continuing any federal arts funding.

NEA Chairwoman Jane Alexander said she was not certain Democrats' fight to save her agency was over in the House, which will vote Monday on the overall spending bill that included the measure to slash NEA funding.
"You may see some changes in this when the entire Interior bill comes up next week. But nobody has seen an up and down vote on the endowment yet, and we feel we'd win that," Alexander told Reuters.

Despite the House moves to close the NEA, advocates of the agency -- which distributes grants to community orchestras, theater groups, film-makers, sculptors, and other artists -- said they expected it would be saved by the Senate and the White House.
"On the Senate side, we're a lot more optimistic that the NEA will be retained," Elliot Mincberg, vice president of the People for the American Way Action Fund, said.

The House voted 217-216 Thursday to back a Republican effort to abolish the NEA by shutting off its funding. Because the vote was so close and because of expected support in the Senate, Mincberg and several House Democrats said they were optimistic the final bill to emerge from Congress would preserve the agency.
The Clinton administration has threatened to veto a $13 billion bill to fund national parks, programs for Native Americans and other programs if the bill killed the NEA.

"The Senate no doubt has stronger support for the arts than the House does," an aide to a Democratic senator said, but she said it may be a struggle to keep next year's NEA funding up at the current $100 million.
House Democrats urged a vote against the Republican block grant plan to better position themselves to carry their fight to the Senate to keep the NEA.
Wisconsin Democrat David Obey called the block grant plan "nothing but a device by which you accomplish the assassination of the National Endowment for the Arts."
But Rep. Vernon Ehlers, a Michigan Republican who sponsored the block grants, said continuing money for arts was more important than maintaining the NEA.
"The NEA has proved to be a lightning rod. It has attracted all types of criticism because they have on occasion given money for art which is profane or obscene or sacrilegious," Ehlers said.

California Republican Sonny Bono, who launched his public career singing with his then-wife Cher, said: "I have been in the arts for 30 years. That has been my occupation. I know of no one in 30 years in the arts who has been assisted by the NEA. So I don't see where the NEA is this amazing contribution to mankind and has brought all these artists forward."

House Speaker Newt Gingrich also made an unusual floor statement to support the block grants, saying they were a way "to take most of the argument, most of the controversy, most of the irritation out of the system, and allow us to focus instead on how do we help the local symphony, how do we help the local ballet, how do we help the local art museum..."
